problemText: A student is writing a synthesis essay on rent-control policy and considers citing an op-ed titled "Why Rent Control Fails," written by the president of a landlords' association and published in a regional business magazine last month. Which statement best evaluates this source's credibility for the essay?
choices: Because the author has an obvious financial stake in the outcome, the source is too biased to cite and should be excluded from the essay entirely
The author's professional stake predicts a slant toward property-owner interests, but the source can still be cited as evidence of how landlords frame the debate, with that stake named explicitly
Because the piece appeared in a business magazine rather than a peer-reviewed academic journal, it carries no evidentiary value regardless of its actual content
Because the op-ed was published so recently, it is automatically more reliable than any older source addressing the same policy question
hints: Every source has a stake; the question is how that stake should shape its use, not whether to throw it out.
Consider what naming the author's position lets a reader do that simply excluding the source does not.

problemText: A source is a memoir written in 1990 by a retired factory worker, recalling in vivid detail a specific conversation that took place on the shop floor fifty years earlier, in 1940. Which statement best evaluates this source's limitations for a synthesis essay?
choices: Because fifty years passed before the memoir was written, any quoted conversation should be treated as reconstructed from memory rather than verbatim, though the memoir remains valuable testimony about the worker's experience

Because the account was written from memory decades after the events it describes, none of its claims about factory life can be trusted at all, so the memoir should be left out of the essay's evidence entirely, even as background

Because a memoir is a personal account, it is inherently more objective than a newspaper report published at the time the events occurred, since its author has had decades to reflect on them calmly and fairly

Because the worker lived through the events firsthand, every quotation in the memoir should be cited as the worker's exact words from 1940, with the vivid detail of the scene serving as proof of its accuracy
hints: Transmission (how a text reached us) is a separate question from whether the source is worth citing at all.
A fifty-year gap affects confidence in exact wording without erasing the testimony's overall value.

problemText: A student's synthesis-essay draft reads: "The company's own sustainability report says pollution has decreased, so I can't use it as evidence." Which revision best reflects a sophisticated understanding of source credibility?
choices: "The company's own sustainability report says pollution has decreased, and this claim can be accepted at face value since companies are legally required to report accurately."
"The company's own sustainability report says pollution has decreased, which proves that no further evidence about the company's environmental record is needed."
"The company's own sustainability report says pollution has decreased, but because any company-produced document is automatically unusable as evidence, this claim will not appear in the essay."

"The company's own sustainability report says pollution has decreased; because the company benefits from appearing environmentally responsible, that claim should be weighed against independent monitoring data rather than dismissed outright."
hints: The original draft commits the naive-bias trap: dismissing a source entirely because it has an interested author.
Look for the revision that names the stake AND still finds a defensible way to use the source.

problemText: A draft paragraph handles two competing nutrition experts by writing: "One expert argues a low-carb diet is best for long-term health, while another argues a low-fat diet is superior. Because the first expert's article was more convincing to me, I will only discuss that view and leave the second expert out of my essay entirely." Which revision best corrects how this draft handles the competing sources?
choices: "...since experts who disagree can never both be right, this essay will cite whichever one is quoted more often elsewhere, treating that popularity as the clearest sign of which expert is correct."
"...because two credible experts cannot genuinely disagree, one of them must not actually be a real expert, so this essay will check each one's credentials and drop whichever seems weaker."

"...the disagreement may dissolve in context: the first expert studies athletic performance and the second studies general cardiovascular risk, so each conclusion likely holds within its own population."

"...the second expert's study will be mentioned in a footnote so that it does not need to be addressed in the body of the essay, keeping the main argument focused and free of distracting counterpoints that only confuse readers."
hints: The original draft commits the false-choice trap: picking a side and dropping the disagreeing source.
Look for the revision that reconciles the disagreement by noticing each source may be right about a different scope or population.

problemText: A student summarizes an opposing historian's view as: "This historian claims the strike succeeded because of union unity, full stop, and ignores every other factor." The historian's actual article states that unity was the single most decisive advantage strikers had, compared with earlier failed strikes, though it also briefly notes that an unusually mild winter reduced strikebreakers' resolve. Which statement best evaluates the student's summary?
choices: The summary straw-mans the historian's position by dropping the acknowledged winter factor and inflating "most decisive" into an all-or-nothing claim
The summary is fair, since a historian's main argument should always be treated as their only argument, and brief side notes like the winter can be set aside
The summary strengthens the essay, since exaggerating an opposing view makes that view easier to refute and so makes the student's own argument look stronger
The summary is unnecessary, since competing historical interpretations should never be mentioned in a synthesis essay that is meant to argue one clear position
hints: Test the summary against the source's actual wording: would the historian recognize this as a fair restatement of their claim?
Notice what the summary quietly drops from the historian's original, qualified argument.

problemText: A student's thesis is: "Remote work increases employee productivity." Which sentence uses a source to QUALIFY this claim rather than simply support it?
choices: A workplace study found that employees working from home completed tasks 15% faster, confirming that remote work increases productivity for employees across a wide range of jobs
A workplace study found that employees working from home completed tasks 15% faster, though a separate survey found this gain largely disappeared for employees with young children at home
A workplace study found that employees working from home completed tasks 15% faster, and every major company should therefore adopt permanent remote work policies for its entire office staff
A workplace study found that employees working from home completed tasks 15% faster, a finding echoed by three additional studies conducted last year across several different industries
hints: Supporting a claim just piles on evidence for it; qualifying a claim narrows its scope or adds a condition.
Look for the sentence that names a specific limit on when or for whom the productivity gain holds.

problemText: A student's overclaiming thesis reads: "Social media has permanently destroyed genuine human connection." A source reports that a 2019 survey found heavy social-media users had LOWER loneliness than non-users when the platform was used mainly for messaging close friends, but higher loneliness when used mainly for passive scrolling. Which revised thesis best QUALIFIES the original claim using this source, without abandoning it?
choices: "Social media has, in fact, strengthened human connection for everyone who uses it regularly, as the survey's findings about messaging close friends clearly demonstrate."
"Social media has permanently destroyed genuine human connection, a conclusion this survey fully confirms by showing higher loneliness among users who scroll passively."

"Because this survey complicates the claim, no argument about social media's effect on connection can be made until researchers produce clearer, larger, and more consistent evidence on the question of cause and effect."

"Social media's effect on genuine connection is not uniformly destructive; the survey suggests it depends on how it is used, undermining connection through passive scrolling but supporting it through messaging."
hints: A qualified thesis keeps its core claim standing while narrowing how far it applies — it is not a full retraction.
Check whether each option still makes a real, arguable claim after accounting for the survey's finding.

problemText: A synthesis essay already cites three sources on the decline of local newspapers, each discussed competently in its own paragraph. To earn the "sophistication" point, a student adds one concluding sentence. Which sentence best demonstrates genuine sophistication rather than mere decoration?
choices: "In summation, it is abundantly clear, as evinced by the aforementioned sources, that local newspapers face myriad multifaceted challenges, the ramifications of which reverberate profoundly throughout contemporary civic life and public discourse in communities across the nation."

"A fourth source, a 2022 industry report, further confirms that advertising revenue has declined, adding one more data point to the pattern already established by the three sources discussed in the body paragraphs above."

"Read individually, each source names a separate cause of decline — but read together, they trace one pattern: each collapsing revenue source pushed newsrooms to cut the local reporting that justified subscriber loyalty, accelerating the next collapse."

"Each of the three sources cited above makes a valid and well-supported point about local newspaper decline, and together they show that the problem deserves serious attention from readers, publishers, and policymakers alike."
hints: Sophistication is a specific stand-back move, not fancier vocabulary or an extra source.
Ask which sentence could NOT have been written after reading only one of the three sources.

problemText: A student claims their essay's final sentence — "This source shows that public trust in institutions has fallen" — earns the AP rubric's sophistication point because it uses the word "multifaceted" and cites a fourth source. Which statement best evaluates this claim?
choices: The student is correct, since sophistication is earned by citing additional sources and using elevated vocabulary, both of which show a command of the material beyond the minimum required

The student is incorrect: the sentence could have been written after reading only one source, so it does not perform the stand-back move sophistication requires, whatever its vocabulary or source count
The student is correct, since any concluding sentence in a synthesis essay automatically satisfies the sophistication requirement once the essay has cited at least three sources

The student is incorrect, but only because the fourth source should have been introduced earlier in the essay rather than at the end, where it cannot be developed into a full body paragraph with its own analysis
hints: Test the sentence against a single question: could it have been written from just one source?
Sophistication requires the sources to be shown in relation to each other, not decorated individually.

problemText: A student's synthesis draft reads: "A peer-reviewed study funded by a beverage industry trade group found no link between sugary drinks and weight gain, so this finding should be excluded from the essay entirely." Which revision best reflects a sophisticated understanding of source credibility?
choices: "...and this finding can be accepted at face value since peer review by itself already guarantees a study is largely free of bias."
"...which proves conclusively that no reputable research has ever found any link between sugary drinks and weight gain."
"...but because the study's funding source has a direct financial stake in the outcome, its methodology should be weighed against independently funded research rather than dismissed outright."

"...but because any industry-funded study is automatically and entirely invalid no matter what its underlying methodology actually looks like in practice, it simply will not appear anywhere in the essay."
hints: Peer review and funding bias are separate questions — one doesn't cancel out the other.
Look for the revision that names the stake AND still finds a defensible way to weigh the source.

problemText: A draft paragraph handles two competing city planners by writing: "One planner argues one-way streets improve traffic flow, while another argues they hurt local business visibility. Because the first planner's article was more convincing to me, I will only discuss that view and leave the second planner out of my essay entirely." Which revision best corrects how this draft handles the competing sources?
choices: "...the disagreement may dissolve once each recommendation is read in context: the first planner studies commuter routes and the second studies retail strips, so each conclusion likely holds within its own setting."

"...since experts who genuinely disagree can never both be right at the same time, this essay will simply cite whichever one happens to get quoted more often elsewhere, in the local press and in city council meetings."
"...because two genuinely credible planners cannot possibly disagree with each other, one of them must not actually be a real expert at all."
"...the second planner's argument will only be mentioned briefly in a footnote so it does not need to be addressed anywhere in the body of the essay."
hints: The original draft commits the false-choice trap: picking a side and dropping the disagreeing source.
Look for the revision that reconciles the disagreement by noticing each source may hold within a different scope.

problemText: A student summarizes an opposing urban planner's view as: "This planner claims congestion pricing works because of reduced traffic, full stop, and ignores every other factor." The planner's actual report states that reduced traffic was the single most significant benefit compared with earlier proposals, though it also briefly notes that lower-income commuters faced a real, if smaller, cost. Which statement best evaluates the student's summary?
choices: The summary is fair and accurate, since a planner's stated main argument should always be treated as their one and only argument
The summary actually strengthens the essay, since exaggerating an opposing view tends to make that view considerably easier to refute
The summary is largely unnecessary here, since competing planning proposals of this kind should never really be mentioned anywhere in a synthesis essay at all
The summary straw-mans the planner's position by dropping the acknowledged equity cost and inflating "most significant" into an absolute, all-or-nothing claim
hints: Test the summary against the source's actual wording: would the planner recognize this as a fair restatement?
Notice what the summary quietly drops from the planner's original, qualified argument.

problemText: A student's thesis is: "Four-day school weeks improve student wellbeing." Which sentence uses a source to QUALIFY this claim rather than simply support it?
choices: A district survey found self-reported stress dropped after switching to a four-day week, confirming that the schedule improves wellbeing
A district survey found self-reported stress dropped after switching to a four-day week, though a separate report found parents' childcare costs rose enough to offset some of that relief

A district survey found self-reported stress dropped after switching to a four-day week, and every single district everywhere should therefore go ahead and adopt this exact same schedule immediately without any exception
A district survey found self-reported stress dropped after switching to a four-day week, a finding already echoed by two additional independent surveys conducted just last year
hints: Supporting a claim just piles on evidence for it; qualifying a claim narrows its scope or adds a condition.
Look for the sentence that names a specific limit on who the benefit reaches.

problemText: A student's overclaiming thesis reads: "Standardized testing has permanently corrupted how schools teach reading." A source reports that a 2021 study found reading instruction narrowed toward test formats mainly in schools facing the threat of state takeover, while schools without that threat showed little curricular change. Which revised thesis best QUALIFIES the original claim using this source, without abandoning it?
choices: "Standardized testing has, in fact, meaningfully improved how schools teach reading for everyone who takes the process seriously enough."
"Standardized testing has permanently corrupted reading instruction absolutely everywhere in every school district, a conclusion this particular study fully and completely confirms."

"Standardized testing narrows reading instruction toward test formats mainly where the stakes of failing are highest, suggesting the corrosive effect tracks accountability pressure rather than testing itself."
"Because this one study complicates the claim somewhat, no argument about standardized testing's effect on reading can really be made at all."
hints: A qualified thesis keeps its core claim standing while narrowing how far it applies — it is not a full retraction.
Check whether the revised thesis still makes a real, arguable claim after accounting for the study's finding.

problemText: A synthesis essay already cites three sources on the rise of food-delivery apps, each discussed competently in its own paragraph. To earn the sophistication point, a student adds one concluding sentence. Which sentence best demonstrates genuine sophistication rather than mere decoration?
choices: Read individually, each source names a separate winner — but together they trace one pattern: the restaurant's reach is financed by a commission that quietly narrows its own margin
In summation, it is abundantly and thoroughly clear, as evinced by the aforementioned sources cited throughout, that food-delivery apps present myriad multifaceted considerations worth noting
A fourth source, a 2023 industry report focused specifically on delivery volume, further confirms yet again that the pattern already established keeps holding
Each of the three sources cited above in this particular essay makes a valid and well-supported point about food-delivery apps
hints: Sophistication is a specific stand-back move, not fancier vocabulary or an extra source.
Ask which sentence could NOT have been written after reading only one of the three sources.

problemText: A student claims their essay's final sentence — "This source shows that gig work has changed how people earn income" — earns the sophistication point because it cites a fourth source and uses the word "multifaceted." Which statement best evaluates this claim?
choices: The student is correct, since sophistication on this rubric is generally earned by citing additional sources and using more elevated vocabulary
The student is correct, since any concluding sentence placed at the very end of a finished synthesis essay automatically and always satisfies the sophistication requirement regardless of content
The student is incorrect, but only because the fourth source should have been introduced much earlier in the essay rather than at its very end

The student is incorrect: the sentence could have been written after reading only one source, so it does not perform the stand-back move sophistication requires, regardless of vocabulary or source count
hints: Test the sentence against a single question: could it have been written from just one source?
Sophistication requires the sources to be shown in relation to each other, not decorated individually.
